name: Diseases – Marine
description: Common diseases of the species in saltwater.json, mapped to each species.
disclaimer: Information collection, not a substitute for a veterinary diagnosis. Many diseases look similar; a reliable diagnosis is often only possible with a microscope. Always use medication according to the package insert or veterinary instructions.
legalNotes: Antibiotics and other antimicrobial veterinary medicines (e.g. metronidazole) have required a prescription throughout the EU since 28 January 2022 (Art. 34(1)(c) Regulation (EU) 2019/6) – obtain only via a veterinarian or pharmacy.
Malachite green is not permitted in food-producing animals in the EU; the information refers exclusively to ornamental fish.
Never dispose of live animals, aquarium water or plants into natural waters (pathogens, invasive species).

fieldNotes.susceptibility: Susceptibility of the species according to sources or group: low, medium, high, very high; for crayfish plague 'possible carrier' (the animal itself usually shows no symptoms).
fieldNotes.contagious.status: yes = transmissible from animal to animal; conditional = pathogen present everywhere, disease mainly in weakened animals; no = not transmissible.

fieldNotes.activeSubstances.invertebrateSafe: false = toxic to invertebrates; null = check manufacturer's information.

diseases.name: Marine White Spot Disease (Cryptocaryon)

contagious.transmission: Direct life cycle: cysts (tomonts) on the substrate release infective theronts that actively seek out fish.
contagious.notes: One of the most common parasites in marine aquariums; without fish the parasite dies off after a while.

diseases.description: Cryptocaryon irritans is the marine counterpart of Ichthyophthirius. It infects wild and cultured fish at 15–30 °C; growth is strongest at 23–30 °C. The life cycle consists of trophont (in the skin), tomont (cyst on the substrate) and theront (swarmer). Susceptibility differs between fish species. Gill-only infection can occur without visible spots – the absence of spots does not rule out Cryptocaryon.
generalSigns: Small white spots, nodules or patches on fins, skin and gills
Flashing, rapid breathing, loss of appetite
With gill infection respiratory distress without visible spots
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically by skin or gill smear.

treatment.summary: Treat all fish in a quarantine tank (copper, hyposalinity or veterinary-prescribed remedies); leave the display tank without fish for several weeks.
steps: Move all fish from the display tank to the quarantine tank – never treat a reef tank with invertebrates with copper.
Set copper to 0.15–0.20 mg/L free copper and check daily with a test kit (UF/IFAS FA165), or
Hyposalinity (strongly reduced salinity) as a control measure described in the literature – not every species tolerates it, invertebrates never.
Run the display tank without fish so the cysts die off; the length of the cycle depends on strain and temperature.
Other substances such as chloroquine only via a fish veterinarian.

activeSubstances.substance: Copper (free Cu²⁺, therapeutic 0.15–0.20 mg/L according to UF/IFAS)
activeSubstances.notes: Only in a quarantine tank without invertebrates, calcareous rock and sand; test daily with a copper test kit. Some fish species are sensitive (e.g. dwarf angelfish). Lethal to invertebrates.

treatment.prognosis: Good with consistent treatment of all fish and a fish-free display tank.

prevention: No untreated fish into the reef tank

diseases.name: Marine Velvet Disease (Amyloodinium)

contagious.transmission: Via free-swimming dinospores through direct contact; fast, simple life cycle without intermediate host.
contagious.notes: One of the most important parasites of marine fish; can be fatal within a short time.

diseases.description: Amyloodinium ocellatum is one of the most important pathogenic parasites of marine and brackish-water fish. The infestation produces a powdery, velvety appearance. The life cycle resembles that of Cryptocaryon but runs faster. Isolates tolerate a wide range of salinity and temperature. Often the first sign is sudden mortality, because the parasite first attacks the gills.
generalSigns: Fine, powdery coating (often only visible in oblique light)
Very rapid breathing, fish stay in the current

treatment.summary: Immediate treatment in a quarantine tank with copper; a freshwater dip gives short-term relief but does not cure on its own.
steps: Move fish to the quarantine tank immediately.
Copper 0.15–0.20 mg/L free copper, test daily (UF/IFAS FA165).
A freshwater dip kills free stages on the fish but is not an effective treatment on its own (UF/IFAS VM90).
Chloroquine only via a fish veterinarian.
Run the display tank without fish for several weeks.

activeSubstances.notes: Only in a quarantine tank without invertebrates, calcareous rock and sand; test daily with a copper test kit. Some fish species are sensitive (e.g. dwarf angelfish). Lethal to invertebrates.

treatment.prognosis: Serious; good only with very early treatment.

prevention: Do not share equipment between tanks

diseases.name: Clownfish Disease (Brooklynellosis)

contagious.transmission: Directly from fish to fish; outbreaks are associated with stress, injuries, ammonia, high temperatures and overstocking.

diseases.description: Brooklynella hostilis is a ciliate that infects the skin and gills of tropical marine fish, initially mainly the gills. Losses have been described in anemonefish, seahorses and other species at public aquariums and importers. Typical is heavy mucus production that peels off in shreds.
generalSigns: Heavy, whitish mucus production, skin peels off in shreds

treatment.summary: Freshwater dips or formalin baths in a quarantine tank (Blasiola 1983).
steps: Formalin or freshwater dips according to expert instructions (Blasiola 1983) – involve a fish veterinarian.

activeSubstances.notes: Baths in a separate container; aerate well.

treatment.prognosis: Good with early intervention, otherwise poor.

diseases.name: Uronema Infection (Scuticociliatosis)

contagious.transmission: Facultative parasite from the water; infects weakened fish and can invade the tissue.
contagious.notes: Often associated with poor water quality.

diseases.description: Uronema is a normally free-living ciliate that infects the skin and musculature of weakened fish and can become systemic. The picture resembles Brooklynella, but reddish, open skin lesions are typical.
generalSigns: Reddish, open skin lesions and ulcers

treatment.summary: Improve water quality and involve a fish veterinarian; skin infection responds to formalin, systemic infection is difficult to treat.

diseases.name: Skin and Gill Flukes in Marine Fish (Monogenea)

pathogen.scientificName: incl. Neobenedenia spp., Benedenia spp., gill flukes

contagious.transmission: Direct life cycle; eggs stick to decoration and hatch later.

diseases.description: Monogeneans are small flatworms on the skin, eyes and gills. They multiply strongly in closed systems. Skin flukes are often almost transparent and only become visible in a freshwater dip, when they turn white and detach.
diseases.diagnosis: Microscopically; skin flukes detach visibly in a freshwater dip.

treatment.summary: Praziquantel in a quarantine tank; repeat because of the eggs. Freshwater dips for relief.
steps: Praziquantel remedy according to the package insert in a quarantine tank.
Repeat the treatment according to the manufacturer.
Short freshwater dip (temperature- and pH-matched) for relief.

activeSubstances.notes: Check tolerance for invertebrates with the manufacturer.

diseases.name: Black Spot Disease (Paravortex, 'Black Ich')

contagious.transmission: Worms leave the fish, continue to grow on the substrate and release up to 160 young worms that immediately infect new fish.

diseases.description: A parasitic turbellarian that in marine aquariums mainly infects the yellow tang (Kent & Olson 1986). The worms appear as small black spots. After three generations, up to 4500 worms per fish were counted; heavily infected fish developed dermatitis with an accompanying Vibrio infection. A formalin bath was effective; neon gobies as cleaners did not help and became infected themselves.
generalSigns: Small black spots on body and fins
With heavy infestation dermatitis, colour loss

treatment.summary: Formalin bath (Kent & Olson 1986); in practice also praziquantel and freshwater dips in a quarantine tank.
steps: Treat the fish in a quarantine tank.
Repeat the treatment to catch newly hatching worms (cycle approx. 10 days).

activeSubstances.notes: Described against related turbellarians (Justine et al. 2009).

diseases.name: Head and Lateral Line Erosion (HLLE)

pathogen.scientificName: incl. activated carbon (lignite-based), diet, water quality

diseases.description: In HLLE, pits and skin lesions form on the head and along the lateral line. The cause is not fully understood. In a study with surgeonfish (Acanthurus bahianus), fish with lignite-based activated carbon in the filter developed HLLE, fish with pelleted carbon did not (Hemdal & Odum 2011); a second study confirms the link with full-stream carbon filtration (Stamper et al. 2011). Rarely fatal, but disfiguring.
generalSigns: Pits and pale skin lesions on the head (around the eyes)
diseases.diagnosis: Clinical appearance; exclusion of other causes.

treatment.summary: Remove lignite-based activated carbon, large water changes, balanced diet; lesions can regress.
steps: Remove activated carbon (especially lignite-based) or switch to washed, pelleted carbon.
treatment.prognosis: Good if the cause is removed; scars partly remain.

prevention: No lignite-based activated carbon with sensitive species

diseases.name: Lymphocystis ('Cauliflower Disease', marine)

contagious.transmission: Via water and contact; symptom-free carriers possible.

diseases.description: The lymphocystis virus causes cauliflower-like white nodules on fins and skin. More than 125 species from fresh and salt water are affected, including clownfish (infections described in A. ocellaris). The nodules usually regress after weeks to months.
generalSigns: White, granular nodules on fins and skin

treatment.summary: No specific therapy; optimise husbandry, isolate the fish.

diseases.name: Fish Tuberculosis (Mycobacteriosis, marine)

contagious.transmission: Via eating infected fish, faeces, water and biofilms.
contagious.notes: ZOONOSIS: skin infections in humans ('fish tank granuloma') – wear gloves. The first detection in 1897 came from a marine aquarium fish.

diseases.description: Chronic, wasting infection with nodules in the internal organs. No treatment with a reliable cure; diagnosis usually only by laboratory examination after death.
generalSigns: Individual deaths over a long period
diseases.diagnosis: Laboratory examination (Ziehl-Neelsen staining, PCR) via a fish veterinarian.

treatment.summary: No reliable cure; humanely euthanise sick fish, hygiene.

recommendedMedications.name: Clove oil (eugenol)
recommendedMedications.legalStatusLabel: not a medicine – freely available (shops, pharmacy, drugstore)

diseases.name: Bacterial Ulcers and Fin Rot (Vibrio and others)

contagious.transmission: Bacteria from the water infect injured or weakened fish.
contagious.notes: Some Vibrio species can cause wound infections in humans.

diseases.description: Vibrios are part of the normal marine flora and mainly infect injured fish or fish weakened by parasites. Vibrio infections accompanied the dermatitis in heavy Paravortex infestations (Kent & Olson 1986).
diseases.diagnosis: Bacteriological examination by a fish veterinarian.

treatment.summary: Eliminate the cause, involve a fish veterinarian; antibiotics require a prescription.

activeSubstances.substance: Antibiotics as prescribed by a veterinarian
activeSubstances.notes: Antibiotics and other antimicrobial veterinary medicines (e.g. metronidazole) have required a veterinary prescription throughout the EU since 28 January 2022 (Art. 34 Regulation (EU) 2019/6) – obtain only via a (fish) veterinarian.

diseases.name: Poisoning by Copper and Fish Medication (Marine Invertebrates)
diseases.description: Most invertebrates are highly sensitive to copper. At the therapeutic 0.15–0.20 mg/L they die; they should only be returned at no more than 0.01 mg/L, ideally 0 mg/L (UF/IFAS FA165). Therefore always treat fish in a separate quarantine tank.

treatment.summary: Immediately large water changes and copper-binding adsorbers.

prevention: Never treat the reef tank with copper

diseases.name: Anemone Bleaching (Loss of Zooxanthellae)

pathogen.scientificName: Loss of symbiotic algae due to heat and light

diseases.description: Anemones with zooxanthellae lose their symbiotic algae under heat stress and turn white. Experiments with host anemones showed bleaching from 27 °C; at 29 °C some animals died, with strong light intensifying the damage.
predisposingFactors: Too strong or suddenly changed lighting

treatment.summary: Lower the temperature, adjust lighting, target-feed.
steps: Bring the temperature into the recommended range (24–26 °C).

diseases.name: Ammonia and Nitrite Poisoning (marine)

contagious.notes: Usually affects all animals in a tank.

diseases.description: Ammonia from waste accumulates in new tanks, after filter failure or with overstocking. Because of the high pH of seawater, a larger proportion is present as toxic free ammonia (NH3). Nitrite is less toxic in seawater than in freshwater due to the high chloride content, but should also not be detectable.
generalSigns: Many animals affected at the same time

treatment.summary: Immediately change water, reduce feeding, check filtration.
steps: Large water change with the same salinity and temperature.

recommendedMedications.name: Water test kits (ammonium, nitrite, nitrate, pH, GH, KH)
recommendedMedications.legalStatusLabel: not a medicine – freely available (shops, pharmacy, drugstore)
